subject: biology

items.q: Which statement about the genetic material of organisms is correct?
items.correct: Every living organism, from bacteria to humans, uses DNA as its genetic material.
items.misconception: Some living organisms use RNA in place of DNA as their genetic material.
items.why: Viruses are studied alongside bacteria as 'pathogens' and 'microorganisms' from GCSE/MYP onwards, so students file them as living things; the existence of RNA viruses then looks like an exception to the rule. Viruses are not cells, cannot metabolize or reproduce on their own, and are not considered to be living. Every living organism, from bacteria to humans, uses DNA as its genetic material; RNA viruses do not contradict this.
items.specStatementText: DNA is the genetic material of every living organism
items.random_wrong: Genetic information in cells is stored in proteins rather than in DNA.

items.q: The influenza virus contains RNA and no DNA. Why does this not contradict the statement that DNA is the genetic material of all living organisms?
items.correct: Viruses are not considered to be living, so the statement does not apply to them.
items.misconception: The virus's RNA is not genetic material; its protein coat carries the genes.
items.why: Proteins are the complex, specific, functional molecules students meet first, and phrases such as 'the gene for insulin' blur the line between the gene and its product. Historically many scientists made the same assumption, which is why the Hershey–Chase experiment was needed. DNA is the genetic material. Genes are lengths of DNA whose base sequence specifies the amino acid sequence of a protein; the protein is the product of the gene, not the gene itself.
items.specStatementText: DNA is the genetic material of every living organism
items.random_wrong: The statement is a generalization, and influenza is one of its known exceptions.

items.q: Which is a correct description of a single nucleotide?
items.correct: A pentose sugar bonded to a phosphate group and to a nitrogenous base.
items.misconception: A nitrogenous base only; the sugar and phosphate belong to the backbone.
items.why: Base sequences are written as strings of letters and the words 'base' and 'nucleotide' are used almost interchangeably in everyday teaching ('a 300-base gene', 'a nucleotide sequence'), so the base becomes the whole unit in the student's mind. Each nucleotide contains a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a base. The sugar and phosphate of every nucleotide together make up the backbone; the base is only one of the three components.
items.specStatementText: A nucleotide has three parts, with the sugar in the middle
items.random_wrong: A phosphate group bonded to a nitrogenous base, which is bonded to a sugar.

items.q: What links one nucleotide to the next within a single strand of DNA?
items.correct: A covalent bond from the phosphate of one nucleotide to the sugar of the next.
items.misconception: A hydrogen bond between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next.
items.why: Hydrogen bonding is the bond type emphasized when DNA structure is taught, so 'bonds in DNA' becomes 'hydrogen bonds' in the student's memory, with no distinction between the bonds within a strand and the bonds between strands. Within a strand, sugar–phosphate bonding makes a continuous chain of covalently bonded atoms, which forms a strong backbone. Hydrogen bonds occur only between complementary bases on the two different strands.
items.specStatementText: Nucleotides link sugar to phosphate to make a strong backbone
items.random_wrong: A covalent bond between the base of one nucleotide and the base of the next one.

items.q: A solution of DNA is heated to 95 °C. The two strands separate, but each strand remains a continuous, intact chain of nucleotides. Which explanation is consistent with these observations?
items.correct: The backbone of each strand is covalently bonded, so it survives heating that breaks the weaker hydrogen bonds between the strands.
items.misconception: Heating breaks the covalent bonds that join the two strands, while the hydrogen bonds within each strand stay intact.
items.why: Students know DNA is durable and know covalent bonds are strong, and reason from stability to bond type; they also carry over the idea that 'bonds between atoms are covalent'. The strands are linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases. Hydrogen bonds are weak individually, which is what allows the strands to be separated for replication and transcription; the covalent bonds are in the backbone within each strand.
items.specStatementText: Nucleotides link sugar to phosphate to make a strong backbone
items.random_wrong: The hydrogen bonds of the backbone are stronger than the covalent bonds between strands, so only the strands come apart.

items.q: Which list names the nitrogenous bases found in DNA?
items.correct: Adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine: four bases.
items.misconception: Adenine, cytosine, guanine and uracil: four bases.
items.why: Thymine and uracil are met as a pair ('U replaces T') and are the two names with no obvious anchor to either molecule, so students remember that one swaps for the other but not which belongs where. Thymine (T) occurs in DNA and uracil (U) occurs in RNA in its place. A nucleic acid containing uracil is RNA; one containing thymine is DNA.
items.specStatementText: Four bases in each nucleic acid form the code
items.random_wrong: Adenine, cytosine, guanine, thymine and uracil.

items.q: How is a molecule of RNA formed from nucleotides?
items.correct: Condensation reactions bond the phosphate of one nucleotide to the sugar of the next, releasing water.
items.misconception: Hydrolysis reactions join nucleotides through their sugars and phosphates, taking in a water molecule each time.
items.why: In everyday language condensation means water appearing (on a cold window), so students associate condensation with water being added rather than released; and 'hydro' in hydrolysis makes it sound like water being involved in building. Condensation joins monomers with the release of water; hydrolysis splits a polymer by adding water. RNA is a polymer formed by condensation of nucleotide monomers, releasing one water molecule per bond formed.
items.specStatementText: RNA is a polymer built by condensation of nucleotides
items.random_wrong: Hydrogen bonds form between the phosphate group of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next in the chain.

items.q: A short RNA molecule is made by joining 20 nucleotides into a single strand. What happens to water during its formation?
items.correct: 19 molecules of water are released, one per bond formed.
items.misconception: 20 molecules of water are released, one for each nucleotide.
items.why: Students count the monomers rather than the bonds between them, because 'one water per condensation' is remembered as 'one water per nucleotide'; the first nucleotide of the chain forms no bond behind it. A linear polymer of n monomers contains n − 1 bonds between them, each formed by one condensation. So n nucleotides release n − 1 water molecules when joined into one strand.
items.specStatementText: RNA is a polymer built by condensation of nucleotides
items.random_wrong: 19 molecules of water are taken in, one to form each bond.

items.q: Which statement describes the structure of a DNA molecule?
items.correct: Two antiparallel strands linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, A with T and G with C.
items.misconception: Two strands with identical base sequences linked by hydrogen bonds between matching bases.
items.why: Both strands are described as 'copies' and as 'carrying the genetic information', and a gene is spoken of as a single sequence, so students assume the second strand simply duplicates the first. The two strands are linked by hydrogen bonding between complementary base pairs, A with T and G with C. Each strand's sequence is the complement of the other's, which is why each can act as a template to rebuild its partner.
items.specStatementText: Two antiparallel strands, paired by hydrogen bonds, make the double helix
items.random_wrong: Two antiparallel strands linked by covalent bonds between complementary base pairs, A–T and G–C.

items.q: Part of one strand of a DNA molecule has the base sequence ATGGCA. What is the base sequence of the complementary strand at the same position?
items.correct: TACCGT
items.misconception: GCAATG
items.why: Nothing at SL gives a reason for the pairings, so students memorize four letters with no rule to hang them on. Those who have met the purine/pyrimidine grouping (A with G, C with T) pair within the group they remember; others simply recall that there are two pairs and reassemble them wrongly. In DNA, A pairs with T and G pairs with C. These are the complementary pairs whose hydrogen bonding links the two strands, and every diagram of DNA should show these pairings.
items.specStatementText: Two antiparallel strands, paired by hydrogen bonds, make the double helix
items.random_wrong: ATGGCA

items.q: Which row correctly gives differences between DNA and RNA?
items.correct: DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, ribose and uracil.
items.misconception: DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, deoxyribose, thymine.
items.why: At GCSE/MYP mRNA is introduced as 'a copy of the gene' that leaves the nucleus, so students picture it as one detached DNA strand and never learn that its sugar and one of its bases differ. There are three differences: the number of strands (DNA two, RNA one), the pentose sugar (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA) and the bases (thymine in DNA, uracil in RNA).
items.specStatementText: How DNA and RNA differ: strands, sugar, bases
items.random_wrong: DNA: two strands, ribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, deoxyribose, uracil.

items.q: A student sketches the ring structures of ribose and deoxyribose. Which difference should the sketch show?
items.correct: One carbon of the deoxyribose ring carries –H where ribose carries –OH.
items.misconception: One carbon of the deoxyribose ring has an extra –OH that ribose lacks.
items.why: Students do not parse 'deoxy' as 'lacking an oxygen' and, knowing only that the two sugars differ by an oxygen, guess the direction; DNA feels like the 'bigger, more important' molecule, so it is given the extra atom. Deoxy means 'without oxygen'. Deoxyribose is ribose with one hydroxyl (–OH) group replaced by a hydrogen atom, so it has one fewer oxygen atom than ribose. In a sketch the difference is shown at that one carbon of the ring.
items.specStatementText: How DNA and RNA differ: strands, sugar, bases
items.random_wrong: The deoxyribose ring has six carbon atoms where the ribose ring has five.

items.q: How does complementary base pairing allow the genetic information in a DNA molecule to be replicated?
items.correct: Each separated strand is a template on which free nucleotides pair by hydrogen bonding, so both new molecules keep the original sequence.
items.misconception: Each separated strand acts as a template on which free nucleotides pair by covalent bonding, so both new molecules carry the original sequence.
items.why: Students know DNA is durable and know covalent bonds are strong, and reason from stability to bond type; they also carry over the idea that 'bonds between atoms are covalent'. The strands are linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases. Hydrogen bonds are weak individually, which is what allows the strands to be separated for replication and transcription; the covalent bonds are in the backbone within each strand.
items.specStatementText: Complementary pairing lets DNA be copied and expressed
items.random_wrong: Each strand is copied directly, base for base, so the new strand is identical to the strand it was built against, preserving the sequence.

items.q: The template strand of a gene has the base sequence TACGGA at one position. What base sequence will the mRNA transcribed from it have at that position?
items.correct: AUGCCU
items.misconception: UACGGA
items.why: The words 'copy' and 'copying' are used for both replication and transcription, and a copy in everyday life is identical to the original. In transcription, RNA nucleotides are added to the growing mRNA by complementary base pairing with the template strand, so the mRNA is complementary to the template, not identical to it.
items.specStatementText: Complementary pairing lets DNA be copied and expressed
items.random_wrong: ATGCCT

items.q: How many different base sequences are possible for a single DNA strand that is 10 nucleotides long?
items.correct: 4¹⁰, which is about 1 000 000
items.misconception: 4 × 10, which is exactly 40
items.why: Students reach for the simplest combination of the two numbers in the question; the idea that possibilities multiply at each position (4 × 4 × 4 …) is unfamiliar unless it has been worked through. Each position can hold any of four bases independently of the others, so a strand of n nucleotides has 4 × 4 × … (n times) = 4ⁿ possible sequences. For n = 10 this is already 1 048 576.
items.specStatementText: Any length, any sequence: DNA's storage capacity has no limit
items.random_wrong: 10⁴, which is exactly 10 000

items.q: The human gene for insulin was inserted into a bacterium, which then produced insulin identical to the human protein. Which conclusion does this best support, and why?
items.correct: The genetic code is shared by humans and bacteria, because the bacterium translated human triplets into the same amino acids.
items.misconception: Humans and bacteria share the same genes, because the bacterium already carried all the information needed to make human insulin.
items.why: Students who have accepted that the code is shared over-extend 'the same' from the rules of the code to the information written in it, again because 'code' and 'sequence' are used loosely. Universality is a statement about the code, not the message: organisms share the rules for reading triplets while having very different base sequences. Shared rules across all life are evidence of common ancestry.
items.specStatementText: One genetic code for all life points to one common ancestor
items.random_wrong: The bacterium adopted the human genetic code in place of its own bacterial code when the human gene was inserted.

items.q: What do the labels 5' and 3' refer to in a strand of DNA or RNA?
items.correct: The carbon atoms of the pentose sugar that carry the phosphate group and the hydroxyl group.
items.misconception: The positions of the first and last nucleotides in the strand, counted along it from the starting end.
items.why: Numbers on a sequence naturally read as positions, and the labels sit at the ends of the strand in diagrams, so students take them as counting markers rather than as atom labels. The numbers name carbon atoms of the sugar (the prime distinguishes sugar carbons from atoms of the base). Each nucleotide has a 5' carbon carrying the phosphate and a 3' carbon carrying a hydroxyl, and the ends of a strand are named after whichever of these is free.
items.specStatementText: Strands have direction: 5' to 3'
items.random_wrong: The names given to the two different strands that together make up the DNA double helix.

items.q: During replication, in which direction is a new DNA strand synthesized, and why?
items.correct: 5' to 3', because nucleotides can be added only to the free hydroxyl on the 3' carbon of the strand.
items.misconception: 3' to 5', because a nucleotide can be added only to the free phosphate on the 5' carbon of the growing strand.
items.why: Students know the template is read 3' to 5' and that the strands are antiparallel, and then apply 3' to 5' to everything; or they simply recall the two numbers in the wrong order. Synthesis of DNA and RNA is 5' to 3' because nucleotides can only be added to a free 3' hydroxyl. The template strand is therefore read 3' to 5', and the ribosome translates mRNA 5' to 3'.
items.specStatementText: Strands have direction: 5' to 3'
items.random_wrong: 5' to 3', because the template strand is read in the same direction as that in which the new strand grows.

items.q: Why does the DNA double helix have the same three-dimensional structure whatever its base sequence?
items.correct: Every base pair is one two-ring purine with one one-ring pyrimidine, so A–T and C–G pairs are of equal length.
items.misconception: Purines pair with purines and pyrimidines with pyrimidines, so both bases in every pair are the same size.
items.why: Students expect 'complementary' or 'matching' to mean 'alike', and the classification into purines and pyrimidines suggests that the members of each class belong together. Each base pair is one purine bonded to one pyrimidine. A purine–purine pair would be too wide and a pyrimidine–pyrimidine pair too narrow to fit a regular helix; purine-to-pyrimidine pairing gives every pair the same length.
items.specStatementText: Purine with pyrimidine keeps the helix a constant width
items.random_wrong: G–C pairs are longer than A–T pairs, but the helix adjusts its width locally so its shape is preserved.

items.q: Which statement describes the structure of a nucleosome?
items.correct: DNA is wrapped around a core of eight histone proteins, held in place by an additional histone attached to linker DNA.
items.misconception: Eight histone proteins are wrapped around a length of DNA, held in place by an additional histone on linker DNA.
items.why: 'DNA packaging' and 'proteins associated with DNA' suggest a wrapping or coating applied to the DNA, and 'beads on a string' diagrams can be read either way if the student does not notice which is the string. The DNA is the string and the histone core is the bead: a length of DNA is wound around the outside of a core of eight histone proteins, and linker DNA connects one nucleosome to the next.
items.specStatementText: A nucleosome: DNA wrapped around eight histones
items.random_wrong: DNA is wrapped around a core of nine histone proteins, one of which is attached to the linker DNA between the cores.

items.q: A student uses molecular visualization software to examine a nucleosome, colouring the DNA one colour and the proteins another. What would the student observe about the association between the DNA and the proteins?
items.correct: The DNA lies on the outside, wound around a compact core of eight protein molecules, with its phosphate backbone against the protein surface.
items.misconception: The DNA and the proteins share covalent bonds at many points, with the backbone of the DNA fused to the surface of the protein core.
items.why: Students reason from the stability of the association to strong bonding, and 'covalent' is the strong bond they know; they have not considered that the DNA must also be able to be unwound for replication and transcription. The association between DNA and histones is non-covalent, based on attraction between the negatively charged phosphates of the DNA and the positively charged histones. This is stable but reversible, so the DNA can be released when it needs to be copied or transcribed.
items.specStatementText: A nucleosome: DNA wrapped around eight histones
items.random_wrong: The proteins lie on the outside, forming a coat around a compact loop of DNA, with the protein surfaces facing outward, away from the DNA backbone.

items.q: Hershey and Chase labelled one batch of bacteriophages with radioactive phosphorus (³²P) and another with radioactive sulfur (³⁵S). Why were these two elements chosen?
items.correct: DNA contains phosphorus but no sulfur, and protein sulfur but no phosphorus, so each label marked one component.
items.misconception: Protein contains phosphorus but not sulfur, and DNA contains sulfur but not phosphorus, so each label marked only one component.
items.why: The student has not connected the labels to the elements in each molecule (phosphate groups in DNA; sulfur-containing amino acids in protein) and remembers the two isotopes as an arbitrary pair. DNA contains phosphorus in its phosphate groups and no sulfur; protein contains sulfur in some amino acids and no phosphorus. So ³²P traces only DNA and ³⁵S traces only protein.
items.specStatementText: Hershey and Chase traced DNA, not protein, into bacteria
items.random_wrong: The labels showed that the phage particles contained both DNA and protein, which was enough to identify the genetic material.

items.q: In the Hershey–Chase experiment, bacteria were infected with labelled phages, the mixture was agitated in a blender to remove phage coats from the bacterial surface, and then centrifuged so that the bacteria formed a pellet. Most of the ³²P was in the pellet and most of the ³⁵S was in the liquid above it, and the new phages produced by the bacteria contained ³²P. What do these results show?
items.correct: Phage DNA entered the bacteria and directed the production of new phages, while the phage protein coats stayed outside them.
items.misconception: The phages are composed of both DNA and protein, and both components are needed for the phage to infect a bacterium.
items.why: Students assume that identifying the molecule present is the same as identifying the molecule responsible; they miss that phages also contain protein, so the experiment had to find which component entered the cell. Phages contain both DNA and protein, so the question was which of the two enters the bacterium and directs production of new viruses. ³²P (DNA) was found inside the bacteria and ³⁵S (protein) outside, and new phages carried ³²P; DNA, not protein, is the genetic material.
items.specStatementText: Hershey and Chase traced DNA, not protein, into bacteria
items.random_wrong: Phage protein entered the bacteria and directed the production of new phages, while the DNA stayed outside.

items.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between technology and the Hershey–Chase experiment?
items.correct: Radioisotopes becoming available as research tools made it possible to trace DNA and protein separately during infection.
items.misconception: Hershey and Chase designed the experiment first, and radioisotope techniques were then developed specifically to carry it out.
items.why: Science is often presented as a sequence of great ideas by great thinkers, with equipment as a detail, so students assume ideas always come first and technology follows. Hershey and Chase could carry out their experiment because radioisotopes had become available to scientists as research tools. The technology opened the possibility of the experiment; this is an example of how technological developments can open up new possibilities for experiments.
items.specStatementText: Hershey and Chase traced DNA, not protein, into bacteria
items.random_wrong: The experiment could have been done at any earlier time; radioisotopes only made the measurements more precise.

items.q: Chargaff measured the percentage of each base in DNA from different organisms. For human DNA he found adenine 30.9%, thymine 29.4%, guanine 19.9% and cytosine 19.8%. For the bacterium E. coli he found adenine 24.7%, thymine 23.6%, guanine 26.0% and cytosine 25.7%. Which conclusion do these data support?
items.correct: In each organism A ≈ T and G ≈ C, but base composition differs between organisms, so DNA is not a simple repeating sequence of the bases.
items.misconception: All four bases are present in roughly similar amounts in both organisms, which is consistent with DNA being a simple repeating tetranucleotide.
items.why: Four bases and a 'regular' molecule suggest equal shares, and simple base-pairing exercises rarely use realistic proportions; this is essentially the tetranucleotide hypothesis that Chargaff's data falsified. Chargaff's data showed A = T and G = C in every organism (purines equal pyrimidines), but the percentage of G + C varies widely between species. Equal amounts of all four bases is the exception, not the rule.
items.specStatementText: Chargaff's ratios falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis
items.random_wrong: The equal amounts of A and T and of G and C prove that DNA is a double helix in which each A is hydrogen-bonded to a T and each G is bonded to a C.

items.q: The tetranucleotide hypothesis proposed that DNA was a repeating sequence of the four bases. Which statement correctly describes the role of Chargaff's data in relation to this hypothesis?
items.correct: Confirming cases cannot prove a hypothesis, but Chargaff's contrary measurements were enough to show it false.
items.misconception: The hypothesis had been proved by earlier supporting measurements, so Chargaff's data could only refine it rather than reject it.
items.why: In everyday reasoning evidence accumulates towards proof, and school science often speaks of experiments 'proving' ideas. Confirming observations can support but never prove a general hypothesis, because it makes a claim about cases not yet observed. Falsification is different: Chargaff's measurements contradicted the tetranucleotide hypothesis, and that was enough to reject it.
items.specStatementText: Chargaff's ratios falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis
items.random_wrong: Chargaff's data replaced the hypothesis with proof that DNA is a double helix with complementary base pairs throughout.

items.q: Which statement best explains why the capacity of DNA for storing information is described as limitless?
items.correct: A DNA molecule can be of any length and have any base sequence, so the number of possible sequences has no upper bound.
items.misconception: Capacity is not limitless: with only four bases, DNA can store far less than a code with more symbols could.
items.why: Students compare the four-letter DNA 'alphabet' with the 26-letter written alphabet and judge capacity by the number of symbols, rather than by the number of positions available. Capacity depends on length as well as on the number of symbols. Any length and any sequence is possible, so 4ⁿ grows without limit; DNA stores an enormous amount of data with great economy.
items.specStatementText: Any length, any sequence: DNA's storage capacity has no limit
items.random_wrong: Each position can be one of only two base pairs, but the molecule is long enough to make up for the small alphabet.

items.q: How are the three components of a nucleotide arranged?
items.correct: The pentose sugar is central: the phosphate group is bonded to the sugar and the base is bonded to the sugar. The phosphate and the base are not bonded to each other.
items.misconception: The three components are joined in a line, phosphate to sugar to base or phosphate to base to sugar, so the phosphate is bonded to the base.
items.why: The circle–pentagon–rectangle convention places the three shapes side by side, and students read a row of shapes as a chain, without noticing that both the circle and the rectangle are attached to the pentagon. In a nucleotide the pentose sugar is bonded to both of the other components. The phosphate is attached to one carbon of the sugar and the base to another; there is no bond between the phosphate and the base.
items.specStatementText: A nucleotide has three parts, with the sugar in the middle
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What kind of sugar is found in a nucleotide?
items.correct: A pentose (five-carbon) sugar: ribose in RNA or deoxyribose in DNA.
items.misconception: The sugar in a nucleotide is glucose, or another six-carbon sugar, because that is what 'sugar' means.
items.why: Glucose is the sugar students have met in respiration, photosynthesis and carbohydrate structure, and the everyday word 'sugar' calls it to mind; a five-carbon sugar is unfamiliar. Nucleotides contain a pentose sugar with five carbon atoms, drawn as a pentagon. Ribose is the pentose in RNA and deoxyribose the pentose in DNA; glucose is a hexose and is not a component of nucleic acids.
items.specStatementText: A nucleotide has three parts, with the sugar in the middle
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which components of adjacent nucleotides are bonded together to form a strand?
items.correct: The phosphate group of one nucleotide is bonded to the pentose sugar of the next; the bases are not involved in linking nucleotides within a strand.
items.misconception: Adjacent nucleotides in a strand are joined through their bases, because the bases are the parts that carry the information and are read one after another.
items.why: Base sequences are read along the strand as a series of letters, and ladder diagrams show the bases in a line, so students imagine the bases connected to each other like beads on a string. The bases project from the sugar–phosphate backbone and are bonded only to their own sugar. The strand is held together by covalent bonds between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next.
items.specStatementText: Nucleotides link sugar to phosphate to make a strong backbone
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many different nitrogenous bases does DNA contain?
items.correct: Four: adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine.
items.misconception: DNA contains five bases, adenine, cytosine, guanine, thymine and uracil, because five base names are learned for nucleic acids.
items.why: Students collect all the base names they meet across DNA and RNA into one list and attach the whole list to DNA, the molecule they think of as 'the' nucleic acid. Each nucleic acid contains exactly four bases. DNA has A, C, G and T; RNA has A, C, G and U. Uracil is not found in DNA.
items.specStatementText: Four bases in each nucleic acid form the code
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In which directions do the two strands of a DNA double helix run?
items.correct: In opposite directions: the strands are antiparallel.
items.misconception: The two strands run parallel, in the same direction, because they are drawn side by side and look like mirror images.
items.why: Simple ladder diagrams show two identical-looking rails, and nothing in a GCSE/MYP treatment gives a strand a direction, so students have no reason to think the two rails point different ways. The two strands are antiparallel: they run in opposite directions. In diagrams of DNA the strands should be drawn antiparallel, with the sugars of one strand oriented opposite to those of the other.
items.specStatementText: Two antiparallel strands, paired by hydrogen bonds, make the double helix
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many strands does an RNA molecule have?
items.correct: RNA is usually a single strand of nucleotides.
items.misconception: RNA is double-stranded like DNA, because all nucleic acids form a double helix.
items.why: The double helix is the iconic image of a nucleic acid, so a student who has not attended to the differences between the two molecules draws RNA the same way. One of the differences between DNA and RNA is the number of strands: DNA has two strands, RNA has one.
items.specStatementText: How DNA and RNA differ: strands, sugar, bases
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many possibilities are there at each position along one strand of DNA?
items.correct: Four: A, C, G or T. The base on the other strand is then fixed by complementary pairing, but the strand itself can have any of the four at each position.
items.misconception: There are only two possibilities at each position, because bases come in two pairs (A–T and G–C) and each position is one pair or the other.
items.why: Base pairs are taught as units, and students count the two kinds of pair rather than the four bases; they forget that an A–T pair can be A on the first strand or T on the first strand. A base pair can be A–T, T–A, G–C or C–G, so each position on a given strand can be any of four bases. This is why the number of possible sequences is 4ⁿ, not 2ⁿ.
items.specStatementText: Any length, any sequence: DNA's storage capacity has no limit
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the genetic code different in different species?
items.correct: No. The same base triplets specify the same amino acids in essentially all organisms; the genetic code is conserved across all life forms.
items.misconception: Each species has its own genetic code, so a gene from one species would be read differently by another.
items.why: In everyday speech 'genetic code' is used to mean an organism's DNA sequence or genome ('cracking the genetic code of the mammoth'), so students conflate the code (the triplet-to-amino-acid rules) with the sequence, which does differ between species. The genetic code is the set of rules translating base triplets into amino acids, and it is essentially the same in all life forms. What differs between species is the base sequence of their DNA, not the code used to read it.
items.specStatementText: One genetic code for all life points to one common ancestor
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is a shared genetic code evidence of universal common ancestry rather than simply chemical necessity?
items.correct: There is no chemical reason why a particular triplet should specify a particular amino acid; the assignments are arbitrary, so their sharing by all organisms is best explained by inheritance from a common ancestor.
items.misconception: The genetic code is the same in all organisms because it is the only chemically possible code, so it would arise the same way in any organism regardless of ancestry.
items.why: Students expect biological rules to be chemically determined, as bonding rules are, and do not realize that the link between a codon and an amino acid is made by cellular machinery (tRNAs and enzymes) that could have evolved differently. The codon assignments are arbitrary with respect to chemistry. Because a different assignment would work just as well, the fact that all life forms use the same one indicates that they inherited it from a universal common ancestor.
items.specStatementText: One genetic code for all life points to one common ancestor
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: To which end of a growing DNA or RNA strand can new nucleotides be added?
items.correct: Only to the 3' end, where the free hydroxyl group on the 3' carbon of the last sugar reacts with the phosphate of the incoming nucleotide.
items.misconception: New nucleotides can be added at either end of a growing strand, so a strand can grow in both directions.
items.why: A chain that is being lengthened seems, by everyday intuition, to be extendable from either end, and the chemical reason for the restriction (the free 3' –OH) is not obvious from a simple diagram. Nucleotides are added only to the free 3' hydroxyl of the growing strand, so DNA and RNA are always synthesized in the 5' to 3' direction. This has consequences for replication, transcription and translation.
items.specStatementText: Strands have direction: 5' to 3'
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are 5' and 3' the names of the two strands of the double helix?
items.correct: No. Every strand has both a 5' end and a 3' end; the labels name the ends of a strand, not the strands.
items.misconception: One strand of DNA is the 5' strand and the other is the 3' strand.
items.why: In diagrams the top strand often shows 5' at the left and the bottom strand 3' at the left, so students attach the label to the strand nearest it. Each strand has a 5' end and a 3' end. Because the two strands are antiparallel, the 5' end of one strand lies opposite the 3' end of the other, which is why the labels appear to belong to different strands.
items.specStatementText: Strands have direction: 5' to 3'
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In which direction is the template strand read while a new strand is synthesized 5' to 3'?
items.correct: 3' to 5'. Because the new strand is antiparallel to the template, building it 5' to 3' means moving along the template from its 3' end towards its 5' end.
items.misconception: The template strand is read 5' to 3', in the same direction as the new strand grows.
items.why: Students forget that the new strand is antiparallel to its template and imagine the enzyme copying along the template in the same direction that the copy grows. Synthesis is 5' to 3' on the new strand, so the template, which runs antiparallel, is read 3' to 5'. This applies to DNA polymerase in replication and to RNA polymerase in transcription.
items.specStatementText: Strands have direction: 5' to 3'
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the width of the DNA double helix vary along its length depending on the base sequence?
items.correct: No. Every base pair is one purine and one pyrimidine, so A–T and G–C pairs have the same length and the helix has the same three-dimensional structure regardless of sequence.
items.misconception: The helix is wider in some places than others because the two kinds of base pair are different sizes; a G–C-rich region is wider (or an A–T-rich region is wider).
items.why: Students learn that the bases are different molecules and that the two pairs differ in some way (for example in bonding), and infer that they must differ in size too; they do not realize that each pair combines one two-ring base with one one-ring base. A–T and C–G pairs have equal length because each contains one purine (two rings) and one pyrimidine (one ring). The helix therefore has a uniform structure whatever the sequence, which contributes to its stability.
items.specStatementText: Purine with pyrimidine keeps the helix a constant width
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which bases are purines and which are pyrimidines?
items.correct: Purines (two rings): adenine and guanine. Pyrimidines (one ring): cytosine, thymine and uracil.
items.misconception: Purines are the smaller single-ring bases and pyrimidines are the larger two-ring bases.
items.why: 'Pyrimidine' is the longer word, so students expect it to name the larger molecule; there is nothing in the names themselves to fix which is which. Purines are the larger bases with two rings (A and G); pyrimidines are the smaller bases with one ring (C, T and U). A useful check: the shorter word names the larger base.
items.specStatementText: Purine with pyrimidine keeps the helix a constant width
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many histone proteins make up the core of a nucleosome?
items.correct: Eight. An additional histone protein, attached to the linker DNA, holds the DNA on the core but is not part of the core.
items.misconception: The nucleosome core is made of nine histone proteins, because there are eight plus the additional histone.
items.why: Students add the additional (linker) histone to the count of the core, because it is a histone and it is part of the nucleosome. The core is eight histone proteins, around which the DNA is wrapped. The additional histone protein is attached to the linker DNA and holds the nucleosome together; it sits outside the core.
items.specStatementText: A nucleosome: DNA wrapped around eight histones
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What did Chargaff's data establish?
items.correct: That in every organism the amount of A equals T and G equals C, while base composition differs between organisms; this falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis. The data did not themselves reveal the structure of DNA.
items.misconception: Chargaff's data proved that DNA is a double helix with complementary base pairing.
items.why: With hindsight, the equalities A = T and G = C are explained by complementary base pairing, so students read the later explanation back into the data as if Chargaff had discovered the structure. Chargaff measured base composition; he did not determine structure. His data falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis, and were later explained by the double helix model, which accounted for A = T and G = C by complementary base pairing.
items.specStatementText: Chargaff's ratios falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis
